Violence against Teachers

By: Anna Teichert | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With multiple incidents of violence against teachers by learners in our schools reported almost daily, teachers live and work in fear and teaching might soon be seen as a dangerous profession.

Unique Selling Point:
The shocking death of a young teacher at a North West school by a learner who stabbed him to death in September 2018, the numerous reports in news articles as well as cell phone videos taken by fellow learners while learners provoke, assault and attack teachers, have turned the spotlight in recent weeks on the violence against teachers, who’s job it is to impart information to learners.

Due to massive recruitment by foreign countries, teachers are leaving South Africa to work abroad. They are often offered up to five times their local salaries, provided with housing, medical insurance, and flight allowances for them and their family as part of the recruitment package. But is that the only reason they are leaving or does the violence in schools play a part?

According to a survey conducted by the Human Sciences Research Council (HSRC) with the Department of Education among more than 20000 teachers at 1380 schools across the country in 2017 twenty percent of South Africa's teachers believe that schools are violent places and suspect their students and are armed.

We find out why teachers are living in fear of violence from learners.

Summary:
Reports in newspapers and online and videos circulated on social media platforms of teachers being assaulted and attacked in schools paint a bleak picture of South African schools. Safety at schools around the country remains a concern despite the Education Department's promise to step up security measures. Should teaching now be regarded as a dangerous profession? We investigate why teachers are living in fear and what measures are taken to put a stop to the violence in schools
Safety at schools around the country remains a concern despite the Education Department's promise to step up security measures.

Legal:
Question: The other videos – except the bookthrowing – she hasn’t blurred. Also for consistency.

Tim: Like the case study – what’s the trend with these things – has there been an increase in the last few years. We must say we are seeing more on social

WG:
The sections don’t flow
We don’t say at the beginning – it doesn’t come across that she was stabbed by a school kid at all. It looks like an ordinary – Grade 4. 15 year old at the beginning
First link doesn’t work well
You need to give context around why the teacher told her to close the book
The link bout living in fear – after the first case study because it sets up what the story is about
SADTU doesn’t add anything
Can’t substantiate – MEC spokesperson joined us – changed script
VO: we spent 7 hours – context
This is across schools.
You need to explain better what the kid was doing to the teacher

STRUCTURAL:
• Missing a narrative device to build from start through analysis to a climax…I’d suggest making the videos pop out of a map of the country -- to show how widespread it is...maybe see if we have establishing visuals of those towns/areas/provinces...ask Lizzie for those
• Classroom cutaways to colour in the story? -- big closeups of chalk/dusters….kids walking (see their feet)...see teacher walking into class
• Start with case study narrating the critical moment between her and the student
• Lose Mac’s first link
• Rather say “In October last…” in VO
• We don’t say at the beginning -- doesn’t come across that the woman was stabbed by a school kid… looks like an ordinary crime
• Missing information to guide the flow -- linking stories across the spectrum
• Slow -mo the video -- too hectic to follow
• Give info on the teacher that was attacked.
• Don’t mention sub judice (sub judice is not a real reason anymore)
• Presenter says ‘this teacher’ but we haven’t seen her yet.
• Give context of why the book was taken
• LINK about living in fear needs to move up -- it sets up what the story deals with
• Take SADTU guy out
• Joined us… not the kind of scripting we use
• Poetic teacher -- give better context -- pop her video out of a map so we know what happened there
• Fix grammar VO “throw him with a book”-- throw book at him
• Need to spell out for the viewer what is happening on the video
• Set up Noche family first -- this is why the video was made...this is what the Noche boy is trying to get his schoolmates to change their ways
• More from Angie
• End with your case studies strongest upsound
• Conference should come later in the story telling

First link grammar?? We can lose the first link
Rather in October last year
“She had a calling …” segway doesn’t work
What are the numbers, statistics, what are the trends – is it on the increase? Or just more videos?
Bus incident – lacks story telling – tell us what happened, where, when how
Graphic of cell phone footage needs a better treatment
Tell us about each incident – who, when, where, why, how
What would cause children to be violent question should come up before Dr lady at conference

Lerato poetry – perhaps use a better upsound from her poem but again explain what we are seeing – what drove Lerato to write that poem? Is she a teacher that has been accosted by a student? What’s the story behind the video?
SDTU – Maluleke upsound about vulnerability should also come up earlier

But is it causing them to emigrate – rather give us the numbers – x number of teachers are immigrating because of the abuse? Not suer if this is even fair so many factors to why they leave

The headboy video – context – is this school one where there is a higher incident of teacher abuse at his school, what made this boy make such a solemn plea to his peers.

Press Release:


Violent Learners
A spike in video clips on social media showing teachers under attack in the classroom is the tip of an iceberg of lawlessness and violence in schools that is leaving teachers desperate for support. Teachers are left defenceless, facing off against large classes of learners, where they are randomly subjected to verbal and physical assault. Carte Blanche questions the consequences for learners who harm teachers, and asks Basic Education Minister Angie Motshekga what can be done to stem the rising tide of violence in schools.
Producer: Anna Teichert
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli
Watch the trailer


Script:


Karin:
Hy het klaar gereedgestaan met die mes. Hy het nie gepraat nie. Ek het nie gepraat nie. Hy het onmiddellik gekap.
He was there, ready with the knife. He did not talk. I did not talk. He immediately started stabbing.
V/O:
Karin Coetzee, a primary school teacher from Edenburg in the Free State, was attacked in her home twelve months ago. She KNEW her assailant – a grade four learner from her class, who was 15 years old at the time.
12
Karin:
Wat veronderstel was om ‘n lekker dag te wees, het rerig lelik uitgedraai en dit het my en my gesin gebreek.
What was supposed to be a nice day turned out nasty and broke me and my family.
V/O:
While in the garden with a friend and two children, a noise in the street distracted them.
7
Karin:
Met die wat ons vir ‘n split sekonde ons rue draai, het hy by die enigste deur wat oop was, agter ons, ingeglip.
In the split second that we turned our backs, he slipped in at the only open door.
V/O:
The boy made his way into the house and grabbed one of Coetzee’s kitchen knives.
4
Karin:
Ek moes veg vir my lewe.
I had to fight for my life.
V/O:
It was a brutal attack. Coetzee was struck repeatedly before she fell. But it did not end there.
5
Karin:
Ek het in my eie bloed gegly met bloed wat van my gesig aftestroom het. Ek het op my knie geval en hy het my in my nek gesteek. En dit het weer gebeur en hy het my weer gesteek. Maar hy het my nie ‘n derde keer gesteek nie. En dit was die Here se genade.
I slipped in my own blood with blood streaming off my face. I landed on my knee and he stabbed me in the neck. It happened again and again he stabbed me. But he did not stab me a third time. And that was by God’s grace.
V/O:
He ran away before help arrived but was apprehended and taken into custody minutes later. Coetzee was left seriously injured.
7
Karin:
Ek het geweet hy het daardie dag gekom om my dood te maak.
I knew he came to kill me that day.
LINK:
Our teachers are living and working in fear! They are confronted with some learners in their classrooms who do not respect them, who might be using substances causing violence. We hear of weapons taken into schools. They feel hopeless and quite frankly helpless.
V/O:
In recent months, social media has seen a spike in video clips showing teachers under attack by learners.

Minister of Basic Education Angie Motshekga has admitted that schools are becoming more violent and dangerous. (Newspaper article, text on screen - “It is quite clear we have a big problem.”)

As a random sample of provinces, Gauteng schools expelled thirty-one learners for assaulting teachers and other staff in the last year.

Limpopo Education officials have handled nine hundred and forty-two cases of serious learner misconduct in the same period.

The picture looks bleak countrywide…
5

7


6


7

3
Panga Video
V/O:
This week at a school in Limpopo nine pupils were suspended after a fight broke out outside its grounds with pupils used what appeared to be pangas.
9
V/O:
In Zeerust in the North West a seventeen your old learner is facing a murder charge after allegedly stabbing his maths teacher Gadimang Mokolobate to death in his classroom in September. It appears Mokolobate had reprimanded the learner while he was standing in a food queue.

Minister Motshekga described the situation as heart-breaking.
14



3
Angie Motshekga:
When now you have murder in the mix, it just destroys all the beautiful things about education. So, it is a very depressing situation that we find ourselves in.
V/O:
For Motshekga the loss of a talented young educator is as devastating as the breakdown of relationships in the classroom.
7
Angie Motshekga:
I mean he hardly worked for six months and he died at the hands of a learner.
V/O:
The tragedy set off a ripple effect throughout the education sector.
5
Angie Motshekga:
In Zeerust it only took this one child to put us in the crisis.
Olerato video
V/O:
In a town in the same province, Olerato Malepe, a primary school teacher, wrote a wrenching poem on a teachers’ plight in a public school.

8
Olerato:
As I enter a class hell, how do I find comfort when they can read my fear?
How can I teach without stammering when I see blood dripping weapons peeking out of their books in front of them?
V/O:
Olerato was devastated by Mokolobate’s death, because she has also been subjected to verbal abuse and even sexual harassment by her learners.
8
Olerato:
How do I speak willingly when there is a lump of fear blocking my voice from reprimanding?
Do I take two steps forward to lean in and wipe a tear?
Do I take ten steps backwards and treble in a rage fear?
V/O:
But it’s not only teachers who have suffered.
3
Bus driver video
Also in September a nineteen-year-old learner suddenly began punching the bus driver while the bus was in motion.
7
LINK:
It was early morning when learners were on their way to school from Lesley to Secunda.
V/O:
The bus was full of screaming school children whose lives were put in danger by the learner’s actions. It appeared he had been left behind at a previous pick-up point and then had to board the bus at the next stop.
14
V/O:
The learner was expelled, and the bus driver filed a charge of assault. The learner’s mother referred us to their lawyer who declined to comment.
8
Book at teacher video
V/O:
This video shows an angry learner throwing her exercise book at the teacher. The learner was apparently studying for another subject during class, and when the teacher asked her to close the book, she refused…the teacher attempted to take the book away…it was then that the learner threw the book at her.

Gauteng Education MEC spokesman Steve Mabona says the Department was taken by surprise by this incident.

24



6
Steve Mabona:
In this case it was very embarrassing actually. We learned about it when it went viral on social media.
V/O:
Mabona claims any transgression of a school’s code of conduct triggers immediate action.
7
Steve:
Then we had to come to the school, through our district office, just to support the teacher and make sure that psychologically we offer that assistance as well.
MacFarlane:
What are some of the steps that are taken to deal with that?

Steve:
Necessary action was taken, the learner was suspended. Subsequently the decision was made to then expel the child.
Lenasia video
V/O:
At a secondary school in Lenasia, a learner is seen mocking his teacher… he goes as far as rubbing the teacher’s buttocks.

8
MacFarlane:
Where are we with that incident there?

Steve:
Look, we don’t really play. When coming to ill-discipline, definitely we will expel. This cannot happen in our space.
V/O:
But despite the department’s assurance, the learner’s disciplinary process has not been completed and placing him in another school will take time.
7
Steve:
Let us have ample child to rehabilitate the child. Make sure that we are satisfied that the child is ready to go into another school.
V/O:
NICRO is one of the oldest NGOs specialising in crime prevention. Social worker Mandla Mnisi says they work with schools to provide anger management and individual counselling.
9
Macfarlane:
What would cause a learner to lose their temper and then turn violent, especially towards teachers?

Mandla:
Children who come from violent communities, they also display violent behaviour at schools. Children who are constantly being bullied at school, then they retaliate. Children who has inconsistent parenting, they are rebellious.
V/O:
Karin Coetzee understands her learners’ challenging backgrounds.
3
Karin:
Hulle word met dagga en drank en baie dwelms groot en dis half normaal, alhoewel dit nie is nie.
They grow up with dagga and liquor and a lot of drugs and it becomes quite normal, although it is not.
V/O:
With rising lawlessness taking its toll on teachers and schools, Minister Motshekga convened an urgent Safety in Schools Summit this month to urge collaboration between stakeholders.
10

Angie Motshekga:
That is the only way it can work. Teachers are in a very difficult situation. Imagine a class of 60. The teacher is all by themselves. So sometimes you need really intermediaries to navigate or negotiate a space.
V/O:
In her key-note address Senior Researcher at the Institute for Security Studies, Chandré Gould said children who had experienced violence were more likely to be violent.
9
Dr Gould:
You see how they struggle to concentrate in the classroom, you see it when they fight with their peers on the playground, you see it when they fight with you.
V/O:
Gould recommended programmes to address the root causes of violence and restore people’s sense of wellbeing.
6
Dr Gould:
But it needs good leadership and it needs partnership between community-based organisation, government social services, South African Police Services even at times.
LINK:
The crisis of school-related violence is now raised to national level. While education stakeholders have a key role to put a stop to it, where do parents and caregivers come into the picture?
9
Angie Motshekga:
Teachers are also not police, teachers are not social workers and teachers are also not NGO’s and councillors, but teachers are also not parents. Parents have to own up.
V/O:
In Karin Coetzee’s case, her attacker’s father didn’t help matters.
4
Karin:
Sy pa het gekom en kom dreig hy gaan kom klaarmaak wat sy seun nie kon nie.
His father threatened to finish what his son had started.
V/O:
Coetzee obtained a Protection Order against the father.
3
V/O:
But one family – in Manzil Park outside Klerksdorp – has a different approach. William and his wife Ellen Notshe believe in teaching their kids respect for themselves.
8
William:
When you respect yourselves, respecting other people will come automatically.
V/O:
As father to two young boys, William believes the responsibility lies squarely on parents’ shoulders.
6
William:
I need to live by example.
V/O:
After the Zeerust tragedy, Atlegang Notshe, who is head boy of his school, addressed his fellow learners.
UPSOUND VIDEO:
So, if they want to resign because of all that? Then what? Without teachers we are nothing!
7
V/O:
Atlegang wants his fellow school mates to learn respect for teachers.
4
Atlegang:
We spend seven hours with our teachers, our “parents”, yes, during the day. Trust me I calculated it. It is seven hours on the point. Teachers have a lot of emotion into their jobs. They sacrifice a lot.
V/O:
The senseless death of the teacher stabbed by a learner has had a massive impact on the education system. Could it become a rallying point to turn things around, or will it be too late…as it is for Karin Coetzee who – after a year – is still on special medical leave, and terrified of returning to the classroom.
13

10
Karin:
Wie is saam met jou in daardie klaskamer om jou te beskerm teen dit wat kan gebeur?
Who is with you in the classroom to protect you?


PROMO’S

Promo #1: 10 sec
Teachers are increasingly confronted by violent learners. Should teaching now be considered a dangerous occupation? (5)
Karin:
Onderwysers is nie meer veilig nie. (3)
Teacher are not safe anymore.

Promo #2: 15 sec
V/O:
Teachers fear for their safety as they face learners who are increasingly violent. A young teacher was even stabbed to death in the classroom by a learner. (9)
Angie Motshegka:
In Zeerust it only took this one child to put us in the crisis. (5)



Promo # 3: 15 sec
Karin:
Hy het daardie dag gekom om my dood te maak. (3)
V/O:
This teacher from the Free State was brutally attacked by a Grade four learner in her home. She is terrified of returning to the classroom. (8)
Karin:
Jy moet op die bord skryf maar jy weet nie wat agter jou aangaan nie. Wie is saam met jou in daardie klaskamer om jou te beskerm teen dit wat kan gebeur? (6)


Promo #4: 30 sec
V/O:
A teacher in North West was stabbed to death by a learner in September. (5)
Minister Angie Motshekga:
But then now you have murder in the mix, it just destroys all the beautiful things about education. (6)
V/O:
Left for dead by a learner after brutally stabbing this teacher in her home, she is terrified of returning to the classroom. (7)
Ek het daardie ding waar ek myself nou beskerm. Dis asof ek nie naby kinders wil kom nie. (6)
V/O:
Why are learners behaving increasingly violent? (2)
Mandla Minis:
Children who come from violent communities, they also display violent behaviour at schools. (4)

Teachers are left defenceless, facing off against large classes of learners, where they are randomly subjected to verbal and physical assault. Carte Blanche questions the consequences for learners who harm teachers, and asks Basic Education Minister Angie Motshekga what can be done to stem the rising tide of violence in schools. Producer: Anna Teichert Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli Watch the trailer Script: Karin: Hy het klaar gereedgestaan met die mes. Hy het nie gepraat nie. Ek het nie gepraat nie. Hy het onmiddellik gekap. He was there, ready with the knife. He did not talk. I did not talk. He immediately started stabbing. V/O: Karin Coetzee, a primary school teacher from Edenburg in the Free State, was attacked in her home twelve months ago. She KNEW her assailant – a grade four learner from her class, who was 15 years old at the time. 12 Karin: Wat veronderstel was om ‘n lekker dag te wees, het rerig lelik uitgedraai en dit het my en my gesin gebreek. What was supposed to be a nice day turned out nasty and broke me and my family. V/O: While in the garden with a friend and two children, a noise in the street distracted them. 7 Karin: Met die wat ons vir ‘n split sekonde ons rue draai, het hy by die enigste deur wat oop was, agter ons, ingeglip. In the split second that we turned our backs, he slipped in at the only open door. V/O: The boy made his way into the house and grabbed one of Coetzee’s kitchen knives. 4 Karin: Ek moes veg vir my lewe. I had to fight for my life. V/O: It was a brutal attack. Coetzee was struck repeatedly before she fell. But it did not end there. 5 Karin: Ek het in my eie bloed gegly met bloed wat van my gesig aftestroom het. Ek het op my knie geval en hy het my in my nek gesteek. En dit het weer gebeur en hy het my weer gesteek. Maar hy het my nie ‘n derde keer gesteek nie. En dit was die Here se genade. I slipped in my own blood with blood streaming off my face. I landed on my knee and he stabbed me in the neck. It happened again and again he stabbed me. But he did not stab me a third time. And that was by God’s grace. V/O: He ran away before help arrived but was apprehended and taken into custody minutes later. Coetzee was left seriously injured. 7 Karin: Ek het geweet hy het daardie dag gekom om my dood te maak. I knew he came to kill me that day. LINK: Our teachers are living and working in fear! They are confronted with some learners in their classrooms who do not respect them, who might be using substances causing violence. We hear of weapons taken into schools. They feel hopeless and quite frankly helpless. V/O: In recent months, social media has seen a spike in video clips showing teachers under attack by learners. Minister of Basic Education Angie Motshekga has admitted that schools are becoming more violent and dangerous. (Newspaper article, text on screen - “It is quite clear we have a big problem.”) As a random sample of provinces, Gauteng schools expelled thirty-one learners for assaulting teachers and other staff in the last year. Limpopo Education officials have handled nine hundred and forty-two cases of serious learner misconduct in the same period. The picture looks bleak countrywide… 5 7 6 7 3 Panga Video V/O: This week at a school in Limpopo nine pupils were suspended after a fight broke out outside its grounds with pupils used what appeared to be pangas. 9 V/O: In Zeerust in the North West a seventeen your old learner is facing a murder charge after allegedly stabbing his maths teacher Gadimang Mokolobate to death in his classroom in September. It appears Mokolobate had reprimanded the learner while he was standing in a food queue. Minister Motshekga described the situation as heart-breaking. 14 3 Angie Motshekga: When now you have murder in the mix, it just destroys all the beautiful things about education. So, it is a very depressing situation that we find ourselves in. V/O: For Motshekga the loss of a talented young educator is as devastating as the breakdown of relationships in the classroom. 7 Angie Motshekga: I mean he hardly worked for six months and he died at the hands of a learner. V/O: The tragedy set off a ripple effect throughout the education sector. 5 Angie Motshekga: In Zeerust it only took this one child to put us in the crisis. Olerato video V/O: In a town in the same province, Olerato Malepe, a primary school teacher, wrote a wrenching poem on a teachers’ plight in a public school. 8 Olerato: As I enter a class hell, how do I find comfort when they can read my fear? How can I teach without stammering when I see blood dripping weapons peeking out of their books in front of them? V/O: Olerato was devastated by Mokolobate’s death, because she has also been subjected to verbal abuse and even sexual harassment by her learners. 8 Olerato: How do I speak willingly when there is a lump of fear blocking my voice from reprimanding? Do I take two steps forward to lean in and wipe a tear? Do I take ten steps backwards and treble in a rage fear? V/O: But it’s not only teachers who have suffered. 3 Bus driver video Also in September a nineteen-year-old learner suddenly began punching the bus driver while the bus was in motion. 7 LINK: It was early morning when learners were on their way to school from Lesley to Secunda. V/O: The bus was full of screaming school children whose lives were put in danger by the learner’s actions. It appeared he had been left behind at a previous pick-up point and then had to board the bus at the next stop. 14 V/O: The learner was expelled, and the bus driver filed a charge of assault. The learner’s mother referred us to their lawyer who declined to comment. 8 Book at teacher video V/O: This video shows an angry learner throwing her exercise book at the teacher. The learner was apparently studying for another subject during class, and when the teacher asked her to close the book, she refused…the teacher attempted to take the book away…it was then that the learner threw the book at her. Gauteng Education MEC spokesman Steve Mabona says the Department was taken by surprise by this incident. 24 6 Steve Mabona: In this case it was very embarrassing actually. We learned about it when it went viral on social media. V/O: Mabona claims any transgression of a school’s code of conduct triggers immediate action. 7 Steve: Then we had to come to the school, through our district office, just to support the teacher and make sure that psychologically we offer that assistance as well. MacFarlane: What are some of the steps that are taken to deal with that? Steve: Necessary action was taken, the learner was suspended. Subsequently the decision was made to then expel the child. Lenasia video V/O: At a secondary school in Lenasia, a learner is seen mocking his teacher… he goes as far as rubbing the teacher’s buttocks. 8 MacFarlane: Where are we with that incident there? Steve: Look, we don’t really play. When coming to ill-discipline, definitely we will expel. This cannot happen in our space. V/O: But despite the department’s assurance, the learner’s disciplinary process has not been completed and placing him in another school will take time. 7 Steve: Let us have ample child to rehabilitate the child. Make sure that we are satisfied that the child is ready to go into another school. V/O: NICRO is one of the oldest NGOs specialising in crime prevention. Social worker Mandla Mnisi says they work with schools to provide anger management and individual counselling. 9 Macfarlane: What would cause a learner to lose their temper and then turn violent, especially towards teachers? Mandla: Children who come from violent communities, they also display violent behaviour at schools. Children who are constantly being bullied at school, then they retaliate. Children who has inconsistent parenting, they are rebellious. V/O: Karin Coetzee understands her learners’ challenging backgrounds. 3 Karin: Hulle word met dagga en drank en baie dwelms groot en dis half normaal, alhoewel dit nie is nie. They grow up with dagga and liquor and a lot of drugs and it becomes quite normal, although it is not. V/O: With rising lawlessness taking its toll on teachers and schools, Minister Motshekga convened an urgent Safety in Schools Summit this month to urge collaboration between stakeholders. 10 Angie Motshekga: That is the only way it can work. Teachers are in a very difficult situation. Imagine a class of 60. The teacher is all by themselves. So sometimes you need really intermediaries to navigate or negotiate a space. V/O: In her key-note address Senior Researcher at the Institute for Security Studies, Chandré Gould said children who had experienced violence were more likely to be violent. 9 Dr Gould: You see how they struggle to concentrate in the classroom, you see it when they fight with their peers on the playground, you see it when they fight with you. V/O: Gould recommended programmes to address the root causes of violence and restore people’s sense of wellbeing. 6 Dr Gould: But it needs good leadership and it needs partnership between community-based organisation, government social services, South African Police Services even at times. LINK: The crisis of school-related violence is now raised to national level. While education stakeholders have a key role to put a stop to it, where do parents and caregivers come into the picture? 9 Angie Motshekga: Teachers are also not police, teachers are not social workers and teachers are also not NGO’s and councillors, but teachers are also not parents. Parents have to own up. V/O: In Karin Coetzee’s case, her attacker’s father didn’t help matters. 4 Karin: Sy pa het gekom en kom dreig hy gaan kom klaarmaak wat sy seun nie kon nie. His father threatened to finish what his son had started. V/O: Coetzee obtained a Protection Order against the father. 3 V/O: But one family – in Manzil Park outside Klerksdorp – has a different approach. William and his wife Ellen Notshe believe in teaching their kids respect for themselves. 8 William: When you respect yourselves, respecting other people will come automatically. V/O: As father to two young boys, William believes the responsibility lies squarely on parents’ shoulders. 6 William: I need to live by example. V/O: After the Zeerust tragedy, Atlegang Notshe, who is head boy of his school, addressed his fellow learners. UPSOUND VIDEO: So, if they want to resign because of all that? Then what? Without teachers we are nothing! 7 V/O: Atlegang wants his fellow school mates to learn respect for teachers. 4 Atlegang: We spend seven hours with our teachers, our “parents”, yes, during the day. Trust me I calculated it. It is seven hours on the point. Teachers have a lot of emotion into their jobs. They sacrifice a lot. V/O: The senseless death of the teacher stabbed by a learner has had a massive impact on the education system. Could it become a rallying point to turn things around, or will it be too late…as it is for Karin Coetzee who – after a year – is still on special medical leave, and terrified of returning to the classroom. 13 10 Karin: Wie is saam met jou in daardie klaskamer om jou te beskerm teen dit wat kan gebeur? Who is with you in the classroom to protect you? PROMO’S Promo #1: 10 sec Teachers are increasingly confronted by violent learners. Should teaching now be considered a dangerous occupation? (5) Karin: Onderwysers is nie meer veilig nie. (3) Teacher are not safe anymore. Promo #2: 15 sec V/O: Teachers fear for their safety as they face learners who are increasingly violent. A young teacher was even stabbed to death in the classroom by a learner. (9) Angie Motshegka: In Zeerust it only took this one child to put us in the crisis. (5) Promo # 3: 15 sec Karin: Hy het daardie dag gekom om my dood te maak. (3) V/O: This teacher from the Free State was brutally attacked by a Grade four learner in her home. She is terrified of returning to the classroom. (8) Karin: Jy moet op die bord skryf maar jy weet nie wat agter jou aangaan nie. Wie is saam met jou in daardie klaskamer om jou te beskerm teen dit wat kan gebeur? (6) Promo #4: 30 sec V/O: A teacher in North West was stabbed to death by a learner in September. (5) Minister Angie Motshekga: But then now you have murder in the mix, it just destroys all the beautiful things about education. (6) V/O: Left for dead by a learner after brutally stabbing this teacher in her home, she is terrified of returning to the classroom. (7) Ek het daardie ding waar ek myself nou beskerm. Dis asof ek nie naby kinders wil kom nie. (6) V/O: Why are learners behaving increasingly violent? metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With multiple incidents of violence against teachers by learners in our schools reported almost daily, teachers live and work in fear and teaching might soon be seen as a dangerous profession.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The shocking death of a young teacher at a North West school by a learner who stabbed him to death in September 2018, the numerous reports in news articles as well as cell phone videos taken by fellow learners while learners provoke, assault and attack teachers, have turned the spotlight in recent weeks on the violence against teachers, who’s job it is to impart information to learners. Due to massive recruitment by foreign countries, teachers are leaving South Africa to work abroad. They are often offered up to five times their local salaries, provided with housing, medical insurance, and flight allowances for them and their family as part of the recruitment package. But is that the only reason they are leaving or does the violence in schools play a part? According to a survey conducted by the Human Sciences Research Council (HSRC) with the Department of Education among more than 20000 teachers at 1380 schools across the country in 2017 twenty percent of South Africa's teachers believe that schools are violent places and suspect their students and are armed. We find out why teachers are living in fear of violence from learners.
metadata.Summary: Reports in newspapers and online and videos circulated on social media platforms of teachers being assaulted and attacked in schools paint a bleak picture of South African schools. Safety at schools around the country remains a concern despite the Education Department's promise to step up security measures. Should teaching now be regarded as a dangerous profession? We investigate why teachers are living in fear and what measures are taken to put a stop to the violence in schools Safety at schools around the country remains a concern despite the Education Department's promise to step up security measures.
